## Functional Programming

Load Libraries
```{r}
library(tibble)
library(tidyverse)
```


### When do you need a function?
Use a function when:
You have a task you want to use more than once
You want to keep your script clean and organized
You want to avoid mistakes with copy and paste
You minimize places where you need to update your code

### Example: Rescaling data
Imagine you want to rescale multiple columns to lie between 0 and 1 using: 𝑥−min(𝑥)max(𝑥)−min(𝑥)
Set up a dataframe with random numbers:

(set.seed) can set it so that you get the exact same number every time.

```{r}
df <- tibble(
  a = rnorm(10), # rescaling all data between 0 and 1
  b = rnorm(10), # 10 means random number, randomly distributed
  c = rnorm(10),
  d = rnorm(10)
)

head(df)
```


### Without a function: Manual rescaling

```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)))
# "a" should have numbers not less than zero and not greater than one
head(df)
```

### Copy and paste for each column

```{r}
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    a = (a - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(a, na.rm = TRUE) - min(a, na.rm = TRUE)),
    b = (b - min(b, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(b, na.rm = TRUE) - min(b, na.rm = TRUE)),
    c = (c - min(c, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(c, na.rm = TRUE) - min(c, na.rm = TRUE)),
    d = (d - min(d, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(d, na.rm = TRUE) - min(d, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
```

Writing it out like this gives room for error, this is why functions are better

## Writing a Function
### Create a reusable rescaling function

```{r}
rescale01 <- function(x) {
  value <- (x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(x, na.rm = TRUE) - min(x, na.rm = TRUE))
  return(value)
}

df |>
  mutate(
    a = rescale01(a),
    b = rescale01(b), # much easier than re-writing this code^ for all of the letters
    c = rescale01(c),
    d = rescale01(d)
  )
```

### Even better!

```{r}
df |>
  mutate(across(everything(), rescale01))
#mutates everything without typing any letters
```
### Anatomy of a Function

Every function has four key parts:
1. Function name — rescale01 describes what it does (rescales to 0-1)
2. Arguments — function(x) lists the inputs
  * Multiple arguments: function(x, y, z)
3. Function body — The { } block containing the code
4. Return statement — What the function returns

#### Example: Fahrenheit to Celsius
Step 1: The conversion formula

```{r}
temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
```

Type out the functions that you need, for unit conversions or whatever else that you can apply to other codes. 

Step 2: Create the function structure

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {
  # code goes here
}
```

Step 3: Add the formula

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function() {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
}
```
^^ This isnʻt going to work yet. "Temp_F" is the variable that will change case by case.

Step 4: Add the argument

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
}
```

Step 5: Add the return statement

```{r}
f_to_celsius <- function(temp_F) {
  temp_C <- (temp_F - 32) * 5 / 9
  return(temp_C) # this is the value that will be returned to you, always in celcius
}
```

Step 6: Test it

```{r}
f_to_celsius(90)
```

### Practical
#### Celsius to Kelvin

```{r}
celsius_to_kelvin <- function(temp_celsius) {
  temp_K <-(temp_celsius+273.15)
  return(temp_K)
}
```


Test it: woohoo!!
```{r}
celsius_to_kelvin(15)
```

### Making Plot Functions

Why turn plots into functions?
If you have a plot format you use repeatedly, create a function to:
* Write it once, use it many times
* Maintain consistency across figures
* Save time and reduce errors
Let’s create a reusable plot function with the penguin dataset:

```{r}
library(palmerpenguins)
library(PNWColors) # pacific northwest colors

pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
  theme_bw()
```

#### Name and Set up the Function

```{r}
myplot<- function() {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type="discrete")
  
  ggplot(penguins, aes(x=body_mass_g, y=bill_length_mm, color=island))+
    geom_point()+
    geom_smooth(method="lm")+
    scale_color_manual("Island", values=pal)+
    theme_bw()
} # within this function, the arguments that we want to change will be x and y
```

#### Add Flexible Arguments
make arguments broad so the function works with any data

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = y, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

#### Test it

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)
# this doesnʻt work because there arenʻt brackets around argument data
```

#### Use curly-curly {{}} for column names
The {{}} operator from {rlang} (part of tidyverse) lets us pass column names as arguments:

```{r}
myplot <- function(data, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
}
```

#### Test again

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = bill_length_mm)
```

#### Test with Different Variables

```{r}
myplot(data = penguins, x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

### Add Different Arguments
Set defaults so users donʻt have to specify everything

```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y) {
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
    theme_bw()
} # Now with this function, you can change the entire data frame from a simple line of code.
```

#### Now you can call it with just the column arguments:

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

#### Layer onto the Function

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm) +
  labs(x = "Body mass (g)", y = "Flipper length (mm)")
```

### Adding Control Flow with if-else

#### the if-else statement
Use if-else to execute different code based on a condition:

```{r}
a <- 4 # a equals 4
b <- 5 # b equals 5

if (a > b) { # if a is bigger than b, f=20
  f <- 20
} else {
  f <- 10 # if its not, f=10
}

f
```

#### Making your function more flexible
Add an argument to toggle features on/off:
```{r}
myplot <- function(data = penguins, x, y, lines = TRUE) { # its automatically on, but can easily turn it off
  pal <- pnw_palette("Lake", 3, type = "discrete")
  
  if (lines == TRUE) {
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  } else {  # if the lines are not equal to true, then no geom_smooth(line)
    ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, color = island)) +
      geom_point() +
      scale_color_manual("Island", values = pal) +
      theme_bw()
  }
}
```

Test with lines (default)

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm)
```

Test without lines

```{r}
myplot(x = body_mass_g, y = flipper_length_mm, lines = FALSE)
```
